title: Turning audio into speech features · Level 2
slo: Describe how a speech recognition system captures and prepares audio.

exercises.question_text: Which statements describe audio capture? Select all that apply.

options.text: It is the first recognition stage.
options.rationale: Audio capture is the first stage in recognition. It supplies the raw digital signal used by the stages that follow.

options.text: It converts analog sound to digital measurements.
options.rationale: The microphone changes analog sound waves into a digital signal. Each sampled measurement is stored as a numeric value.
Predicting phonemes is acoustic modeling. Audio capture only creates the digital signal.
options.better_fit: Choose this for the stage that uses MFCC feature vectors to estimate phoneme probabilities.

feedback.intrinsic: A call recording would be mislabeled before its sounds could be identified.
feedback.instructional: Keep capture and prediction separate: capture digitizes sound; acoustic modeling predicts phonemes.

options.text: It creates audio from written text.
options.rationale: Creating audio from written text is speech synthesis. Audio capture moves in the opposite direction, from sound to digital measurements.
options.better_fit: Choose this for speech synthesis, such as reading a notification aloud.

feedback.intrinsic: The work would focus on speaking a message instead of collecting what the caller said.
feedback.instructional: Audio capture begins with spoken sound, not written text.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Audio capture is the first stage and turns analog sound into numeric digital measurements.

exercises.question_text: What range commonly balances clarity and efficiency for speech recognition?

options.rationale: Speech recognition commonly balances clarity and efficiency at about 8–16 kHz. This range needs less processing than a higher music rate while retaining useful speech clarity.

options.error_type: Confuses sampling rate with frame duration
options.rationale: 20–30 milliseconds describes the length of an MFCC audio frame. It is a duration, not a number of samples per second.
options.better_fit: Choose this when describing how audio is divided during MFCC extraction.

feedback.intrinsic: The team would set a frame length when it needed to choose a recording rate.
feedback.instructional: kHz measures samples per second. Milliseconds measure the duration of one audio frame.

options.error_type: Confuses rate with MFCC vector size
options.rationale: Thirteen is a common number of values in one MFCC feature vector. It does not describe sampling rate.
options.better_fit: Choose this when describing the usual size of one MFCC vector for a frame.

feedback.intrinsic: The recording would have no meaningful rate setting from this number.
feedback.instructional: A sampling rate is measured in kHz; coefficients summarize an already prepared frame.

options.error_type: Confuses music detail with common speech balance
options.rationale: 44.1 kHz captures more detail and is typical for music. It also requires more processing than the common speech balance.
options.better_fit: Choose this when extra music detail is needed.

feedback.intrinsic: A basic voice-command feature could use more processing than necessary.
feedback.instructional: For common speech recognition, about 8–16 kHz balances clarity and efficiency.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Speech commonly uses about 8–16 kHz to balance clarity with efficient processing.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The feature preparation steps would not produce the intended compact representation.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: First make short frames, then reveal pitches, adjust them for human hearing, and compute the coefficients.

exercises.correct_answer: Split into frames apply Fourier transform map to Mel scale compute coefficients
exercises.explanation: Frames must exist before their frequencies can be analyzed. Frequency information is then mapped to the Mel scale before compact coefficients are computed.

exercises.question_text: A rate of 44.1 kHz captures more detail but needs more ___.

parts.text: A rate of 44.1 kHz captures more detail but needs more

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The trade-off would be incomplete when planning audio capture.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: The added detail requires processing. Sampling names the measurement process, and latency is a timing expectation.

exercises.explanation: A higher rate produces more measurements and therefore more information to handle. That is why it requires more processing.

exercises.question_text: A developer is preparing recorded speech for a meeting-transcription service. Which actions should they take to build MFCC features? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: MFCC extraction begins with overlapping 20–30 millisecond frames. This provides short sections of audio for analysis.

options.text: Reveal pitches with a Fourier transform.
options.rationale: A Fourier transform reveals the pitches in each frame by moving to the frequency domain. This is a required MFCC extraction step.

options.text: Compute a small set of coefficients.
options.rationale: MFCC extraction computes a small set of numbers that summarizes each frame's spectral shape. Often, one vector has 13 values.

options.text: Generate raw audio with a vocoder.
options.error_type: Confuses MFCC extraction with speech synthesis
options.rationale: A vocoder generates waveforms from mel-spectrograms during speech synthesis. It is not used to prepare recorded speech into MFCC features.
options.better_fit: Choose this when generating spoken audio from phonemes and prosody specifications.

feedback.intrinsic: The meeting recording would be turned toward audio creation instead of transcription preparation.
feedback.instructional: MFCC work analyzes incoming recorded audio. Vocoding creates audible output in synthesis.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Build MFCC features by framing the audio, revealing its pitches, using Mel mapping, and computing compact coefficients.

exercises.question_text: A team is adding speech recognition to a hands-free voice-command assistant and must balance clarity with efficient processing. Which choices fit? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use a speech rate around 8–16 kHz.
options.rationale: About 8–16 kHz commonly balances clarity and efficiency for speech recognition. It fits a hands-free voice-command use case.

options.text: Expect higher rates to need more processing.
options.rationale: Higher rates create more audio detail. That additional detail requires more processing.

options.text: Use 44.1 kHz when extra music detail is needed.
options.rationale: 44.1 kHz is a higher rate commonly used for music. It is suitable when extra detail is needed and added processing is acceptable.

options.error_type: Confuses sampling rate with noise reduction
options.rationale: Sampling rate changes how often audio is measured, not whether microphone noise disappears. Background noise and microphone quality affect accuracy directly.
options.better_fit: Choose noise reduction when applying filters to remove hums, clicks, or background noise.

feedback.intrinsic: Voice commands may remain unclear in a noisy room.
feedback.instructional: Do not rely on rate to solve noise. Rate balances detail and processing; filtering addresses unwanted sound.

exercises.explanation: Correct. The common speech range balances clarity and efficiency, while higher rates bring both more detail and more processing.

exercises.question_text: Reconstruct the statement from the pieces.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The definition of a recording setting would be unclear.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Start with sampling rate, then state that it counts audio measurements per second.

exercises.correct_answer: Sampling rate counts audio measurements per second
exercises.explanation: Sampling rate names how many audio measurements are taken in one second. It is measured in hertz, often kilohertz for speech.

exercises.question_text: A common compact speech feature representation is ___.

parts.text: A common compact speech feature representation is

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The next recognition stage would be described with the wrong kind of information.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: MFCCs are compact recognition features. A mel-spectrogram is used in synthesis, phonemes are speech sounds, and 16 kHz is a sampling rate.

exercises.explanation: MFCCs summarize the spectral shape of short audio frames in a compact form. They become the input for acoustic modeling.

exercises.question_text: A voice assistant cannot recognize a user's command because the team has not yet created a digital audio signal. What should the developer do first?

options.text: Capture microphone sound as digital measurements
options.rationale: Recognition needs a digital signal before it can prepare features or predict sounds. A microphone provides that signal by sampling sound waves into numeric measurements.
MFCC vectors are made from captured digital audio. Without a digital signal, there is no waveform to transform into features.
options.better_fit: Choose this after microphone capture when raw audio needs compact speech features.

feedback.intrinsic: The team could not create features because there is no recorded digital waveform.
feedback.instructional: MFCC preparation follows capture. First collect microphone sound as numeric measurements.

options.rationale: Phoneme prediction requires prepared feature vectors. It cannot begin before audio has been captured and prepared.
options.better_fit: Choose this after feature extraction when identifying likely speech sounds.

feedback.intrinsic: The command's sound units could not be estimated from missing audio.
feedback.instructional: First capture the voice, then prepare features, then predict phonemes.

options.rationale: Generating a waveform is part of speech synthesis from text. The situation requires recognizing incoming speech.
options.better_fit: Choose this when the assistant needs to speak a response aloud.

feedback.intrinsic: The assistant would produce audio instead of receiving the user's command.
feedback.instructional: Incoming voice recognition starts with microphone capture; waveform generation is for spoken output.

exercises.explanation: Correct. The first need is microphone capture, which creates the numeric digital audio signal.

exercises.question_text: A ___ changes an audio frame from the time domain to the frequency domain.

parts.text: changes an audio frame from the time domain to the frequency domain.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The frequency-analysis step would be missing from feature preparation.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Use a Fourier transform for time-to-frequency conversion. The Mel scale adjusts resulting frequencies, while MFCCs are compact coefficients.

exercises.explanation: The Fourier transform exposes the pitches in a short audio frame by expressing it in the frequency domain. Mel mapping comes after that conversion.

exercises.question_text: A service center wants to transcribe customer calls, but its recognition system is slowed by raw audio data. What should the engineer use next?

options.rationale: MFCC pre-processing changes raw audio into a compact representation. This makes the information more efficient for pattern recognition while retaining useful speech characteristics.

options.error_type: Confuses feature extraction with sampling-rate choice
options.rationale: A higher rate captures more detail but requires more processing. It does not make raw audio compact.
options.better_fit: Choose this when deciding how much recording detail is needed, especially for music.

feedback.intrinsic: The call data could become even more demanding to process.
feedback.instructional: For compact recognition input, use MFCC pre-processing rather than increasing the sampling rate.

options.error_type: Confuses feature preparation with acoustic modeling
options.rationale: A phoneme prediction model needs feature vectors as input. It does not replace the feature-preparation step.
options.better_fit: Choose this after MFCC extraction to estimate which phoneme occurs at each moment.

feedback.intrinsic: The model would still face unprepared raw audio rather than compact features.
feedback.instructional: Prepare MFCC features first; acoustic modeling then predicts phoneme probabilities from them.

options.rationale: A neural vocoder converts mel-spectrograms into audio waveforms for speech synthesis. Call transcription needs speech recognition preparation instead.
options.better_fit: Choose this when generating spoken audio from text.

feedback.intrinsic: The service center would generate audio rather than make call transcription more efficient.
feedback.instructional: Use MFCC pre-processing for incoming calls. Vocoding belongs to spoken output.

exercises.explanation: Correct. MFCC pre-processing creates compact features that are more efficient for recognition than raw audio.

exercises.question_text: An engineer is improving speech recognition for a voice-controlled vehicle. They need to identify the pitches in each short audio frame before Mel mapping. Which step should they choose?

options.rationale: A Fourier transform reveals the pitches present in each short audio frame. Mel mapping follows this frequency analysis.

options.error_type: Confuses frequency analysis with later coefficient extraction
options.rationale: Coefficient computation comes after frequency analysis and Mel mapping. It cannot identify pitches before those earlier steps.
options.better_fit: Choose this at the end of MFCC extraction after Mel-scale mapping.

feedback.intrinsic: The engineer would skip the step needed to reveal the frame's pitches.
feedback.instructional: Use Fourier analysis first. Then map frequencies to the Mel scale and compute coefficients.

options.error_type: Confuses frame analysis with audio capture
options.rationale: Microphone capture creates the original digital audio signal. The situation already has short frames and needs frequency analysis.
options.better_fit: Choose this at the start, before audio can be divided into frames.

feedback.intrinsic: The preparation would repeat the first stage instead of analyzing the available frames.
feedback.instructional: Capture happens first. Once frames exist, apply a Fourier transform to find their pitches.

options.error_type: Confuses recognition analysis with synthesis representation
options.rationale: A mel-spectrogram is a sound-frequency representation used in speech synthesis before vocoding. It is not a waveform, and this task needs recognition-side Fourier analysis.
options.better_fit: Choose a mel-spectrogram during synthesis when phonemes and prosody are converted toward audio output.

feedback.intrinsic: The vehicle feature would move toward producing audio instead of identifying incoming speech pitches.
feedback.instructional: For recognition frames, use a Fourier transform before Mel mapping. Waveforms are generated later in speech synthesis.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Apply a Fourier transform first to reveal the pitches in each frame, then map frequencies to the Mel scale.
